resources.title: Set Theory Essentials for Relational Databases
resources.content_snippet: Relational algebra treats tables as sets of tuples. UNION combines rows from both sets (eliminating duplicates), INTERSECT extracts only overlapping rows, and EXCEPT/MINUS returns elements in the first set but absent from the second. The Cartesian Product (CROSS JOIN) forms all possible ordered pairs (A x B). Understanding set operations is essential before mastering relational joins.

resources.title: Primary Keys, Foreign Keys & Referential Integrity
resources.content_snippet: A Primary Key uniquely identifies each row in a table (non-null and unique). A Foreign Key in a child table points directly to the Primary Key of a parent table, establishing a 1-to-many or 1-to-1 relationship. Foreign Key constraints enforce referential integrity: you cannot insert a foreign key value that does not exist in the parent table, and you cannot delete a parent record if child records still reference it (without ON DELETE CASCADE).

resources.title: SQL Query Order of Execution (FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY)
resources.content_snippet: SQL queries are NOT executed in the order they are written! The database engine executes in this strict sequence: 1. FROM & JOINs (get data) -> 2. WHERE (filter rows) -> 3. GROUP BY (aggregate) -> 4. HAVING (filter groups) -> 5. SELECT (choose columns/aliases) -> 6. DISTINCT -> 7. ORDER BY (sort) -> 8. LIMIT / OFFSET. This is why column aliases defined in SELECT cannot be used inside WHERE clauses.

resources.title: Visual Guide to SQL Joins: INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL OUTER
resources.content_snippet: INNER JOIN returns only rows with matches in both tables (intersection). LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table, plus matched rows from the right table; if no match exists, the right side returns NULL. FULL OUTER JOIN combines all rows from both tables, populating NULLs on either side when no match is found. Best practice: always verify which column uniquely joins the tables (e.g. ON c.id = o.customer_id) to avoid accidental Cartesian products.

resources.title: Hands-on Practice: Multi-Table Joins & NULL Filtering
resources.content_snippet: Real-world query pattern: To find customers who NEVER placed an order, perform a LEFT JOIN and filter for NULL foreign keys: SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.id IS NULL; This 'Anti-Join' pattern is critical for churn analysis and data quality auditing.

resources.title: GROUP BY and HAVING: Filtering Aggregated Metrics
resources.content_snippet: Aggregation collapses multiple rows into a single summary row using functions like COUNT(), SUM(), AVG(), MIN(), MAX(). Any non-aggregated column in the SELECT clause MUST appear in the GROUP BY clause. Crucial distinction: WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping (operates on raw records), while HAVING filters aggregated metrics AFTER grouping (e.g. HAVING COUNT(order_id) > 10).

resources.title: Advanced SQL Analytics: Window Functions (OVER, PARTITION BY, RANK)
resources.content_snippet: Unlike GROUP BY, window functions perform calculations across a set of rows without collapsing the result into a single row. Syntax: FUNCTION() OVER (PARTITION BY group_col ORDER BY sort_col). Key window functions: ROW_NUMBER() assigns a unique sequential integer; RANK() assigns ranks with gaps for ties (1, 2, 2, 4); DENSE_RANK() assigns ranks without gaps (1, 2, 2, 3); LAG() and LEAD() fetch values from previous or subsequent rows for period-over-period growth calculations.

resources.title: Pandas DataFrames & Series: Indexing and Selection
resources.content_snippet: A Series is a 1D labeled array; a DataFrame is a 2D tabular structure composed of aligned Series. Primary indexing rules: df.loc[rows, cols] uses explicit labels/names (inclusive of stop slice); df.iloc[rows, cols] uses 0-based integer positions (exclusive of stop slice). For boolean filtering, always enclose separate conditions in parentheses: df[(df['age'] > 25) & (df['dept'] == 'Sales')].

resources.title: Data Imputation and Missing Value Strategies in Pandas
resources.content_snippet: Missing data (NaN/None) handling strategies: 1. Dropping with df.dropna(subset=['col'], how='any'). 2. Imputation with df.fillna(). For symmetric normal distributions, impute with the mean. For skewed distributions with heavy outliers, impute with the median. For categorical data, impute with the mode or a dedicated 'Unknown' category. Always check missing proportions first with df.isnull().mean() * 100.

resources.title: Summary Statistics: Skewness, Variance and the Interquartile Range
resources.content_snippet: Summary statistics quantify central tendency and dispersion. In symmetric bell curves, Mean = Median = Mode. In right-skewed distributions (e.g. income), extreme high values pull the Mean to the right: Mean > Median > Mode. Dispersion is measured by Standard Deviation (sensitive to outliers) and Interquartile Range (IQR = Q3 - Q1, robust to outliers). Outlier detection threshold: Values < Q1 - 1.5*IQR or > Q3 + 1.5*IQR.

resources.title: Hypothesis Testing, P-Values, and Statistical Significance
resources.content_snippet: Hypothesis testing evaluates whether an observed effect is real or due to random sampling chance. Null Hypothesis (H0): No effect / no difference. Alternative Hypothesis (H1): There is a significant effect. P-value: Probability of observing data at least as extreme as ours assuming H0 is true. Decision rule: If p-value < alpha (typically 0.05), reject H0. Type I Error: False Positive (rejecting true H0). Type II Error: False Negative (failing to reject false H0).

resources.title: Data Visualization Chart Chooser: Principles of Visual Perception
resources.content_snippet: Matching data types to chart types: 1. Comparisons across categories -> Bar Chart (horizontal if labels are long). 2. Continuous changes over time -> Line Chart. 3. Correlation between two continuous variables -> Scatter Plot. 4. Distribution of a single continuous variable -> Histogram or Box Plot. 5. Composition / Part-to-whole -> Stacked Bar or Treemap (avoid Pie Charts with > 5 slices due to poor human angle perception).

resources.title: Dashboard Design Best Practices: Progressive Disclosure and KPI Hierarchy
resources.content_snippet: Executive dashboard design rules: 1. Place the most critical North Star KPI cards at the top-left (natural F-pattern reading). 2. Use Progressive Disclosure: top-level trends first, with interactive click-through filters for underlying details. 3. Maximize the Data-Ink Ratio (Edward Tufte): remove 3D effects, unnecessary gridlines, and visual clutter. 4. Use color purposefully: monochromatic palettes with an intentional accent color for alerts.
